**Case Vignette: Michael**

Michael is a 21-year-old married man who works as a social ministry coordinator for a small, faith-based humanitarian organization. He presents as earnest, soft-spoken, and physically tense, frequently rubbing his palms against his thighs during sessions. He has been married for eight months to his wife, Chloe, whom he describes as his "anchor."

Michael’s trauma began nine months ago, when he volunteered for a three-month relief deployment to a conflict zone in Eastern Europe. He had just graduated from a ministry training program and felt a deep calling to serve. His role was to coordinate the distribution of food, water, and medical supplies to displaced families in a region near active shelling. For the first six weeks, the work was exhausting but meaningful. He lived in a shared bunker with other aid workers, slept in shifts, and learned to identify the sound of incoming artillery.

The event that changed everything occurred on a Tuesday afternoon. Michael was riding in a supply truck with two local drivers, heading to a village that had been cut off for days. The road was a muddy track through a forest. He remembers the silence before the blast—the absence of birds. Then the world turned white and black. The truck hit an improvised explosive device. Michael was thrown from the vehicle. He landed in a ditch, his ears ringing, his vision blurred. He remembers crawling toward the truck, seeing the driver's body slumped over the wheel, and the other man screaming for help from under twisted metal. Michael tried to pull him out, but his hands were wet with blood and he couldn't get a grip. He stayed with the man until a medical evacuation team arrived, holding his hand, listening to his breathing slow and then stop.

Since returning home six months ago, Michael has not been able to talk about that afternoon. He tells me he "left that part of himself over there." He avoids all news coverage of the war, changes the channel when conflict is mentioned, and has stopped attending the weekly prayer group he used to lead because someone there asked him about his experience. He says his mind goes "blank" when he tries to recall details of his deployment, yet he is haunted by fragments: the smell of diesel and wet earth, the sensation of grit in his mouth, the sound of a man's last breath.

Sleep is a battleground. Michael wakes three to four times a night, drenched in sweat, his heart pounding. He has recurrent nightmares of being trapped in a burning vehicle, but he cannot remember the full dream upon waking—only the terror. He has begun sleeping on the couch so as not to disturb Chloe, who has started crying because she feels he is "already gone." He feels a constant low-grade irritability, snapping at Chloe for small things like leaving the lights on, then feeling overwhelming shame. He has stopped driving on rural roads, taking long detours to avoid the sight of a particular stretch of highway that reminds him of the forest track.

At work, Michael is functional but detached. He organizes donation drives and writes grant proposals, but he feels nothing when he reads letters from families thanking him. He describes a "glass wall" between himself and his emotions. He once loved the work; now he goes through the motions, feeling numb and guilty for being numb. His PCL-5 score is 47, indicating a high level of PTSD symptoms.

He came to therapy at Chloe's urging, after she found him standing in the backyard at 3 a.m., staring at the fence, unable to explain what he was doing. He says he wants to feel "real" again, but he is terrified that if he opens the door to his memories, he will not be able to close it.
